title: The Wage and the Worker
subtitle: What Scripture says about work, wages, debt, and the dignity of the laborer.
question: If God hears the cry of the unpaid harvester, why does the church so often sound like the landowner?
whyItMatters: Most people meet the world through their work before they ever meet it through a creed. The first question a skeptic asks is rarely about the resurrection. It is whether the God you preach notices the woman cleaning the office at midnight. Scripture says He does. The church has too often acted as though He does not.
biblicalFoundation: The wage is not a side issue in the Torah. It is a fault line. 'You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy, whether he is one of your brothers or one of the sojourners. You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets, for he is poor and counts on it' (Deuteronomy 24, paraphrased). Note the reason given. He counts on it. The day laborer in the ancient world had no savings, no margin, no second account. The wage held overnight was bread taken from a table that night. God writes this into law not as charity but as justice owed.

James, writing to scattered churches under pressure, does not soften it. 'Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of hosts' (James 5, paraphrased). The withheld wage has a voice. It does not petition the worker. It petitions God directly, and it reaches Him. James addresses the rich oppressor not with a strategy but with a warning. The gold has rusted. The rust will be a witness.

But work itself begins before the fall, not after it. In Eden the man is placed in the garden 'to work it and keep it' before a single thorn exists. Labor is not the curse. Labor is the dignity given to a creature made in the image of a working God who made and then called it good. The curse makes work hard. It does not make work shameful. This is the ground the prophets stand on when they defend the worker. They are not defending the weak out of pity. They are defending the image of God in a person whose hands are being treated as disposable.

And the law would not let debt become a permanent class. The sabbatical release cancelled debts every seventh year. The Jubilee returned land to families who had lost it. Israel was forbidden to build a society where the poor stayed poor forever and the lender held a man's life as collateral. The point was not equal outcomes. The point was that no human being could be permanently owned by what he owed. We have not kept that law. We have built the machinery that the Jubilee was written to break.

churchRecord.led: When the worker had no other voice, Christians sometimes became the voice. Lord Shaftesbury, an evangelical, spent decades in Parliament fighting the factory conditions that broke children in the mills. The abolition of the slave trade ran through a Clapham faith that refused to call a man property. The early labor movements in Britain and America were soaked in Methodist hymns and chapel preaching, where the dignity of the laborer was first learned on a Sunday before it was ever demanded on a Monday.
churchRecord.failed: And the same church blessed the mill owner and ignored the millhand. It preached patience to the man with no wage and prosperity to the man who withheld it. It read 'slaves obey your masters' to people in chains and skipped the verse that warned the masters. It built sanctuaries on cotton money and asked no questions about the hands that picked it. The church has stood on both sides of this. We do not get to pretend we were only ever on one.

whereWeAgree: The worker bears the image of God, and exploitation of the worker is not an economic inefficiency to be corrected later. It is sin that God hears and answers. On this the whole of Scripture is unembarrassed and loud.
captureLeft: The left can shrink the worker into a category. The person with a name and a calling becomes a unit of class grievance, and his labor becomes only a site of conflict rather than a place of dignity. It can also locate all hope in the state, as if justice arrives by statute alone and the human heart that withholds the wage needs no repentance, only regulation.
captureRight: The right can baptize the market as if its outcomes were providence, treating whatever wage clears as therefore just. It can hear every concern for the worker as envy, every call for mercy as theft, and quote the parts of Paul about diligence while never reaching the parts of James about fraud. It mistakes the freedom to accumulate for the will of God.
whereWeDiffer: Christians who agree the worker has dignity will still disagree, honestly, about means. Minimum wage law, union power, the size of the state, how markets set prices, what a government owes and what it wrecks when it overreaches. These are real arguments about prudence, and Scripture does not hand us a policy. It hands us a concern we are forbidden to abandon while we argue.
theCost: To take this seriously is to look at your own arrangements first. The wage you pay the cleaner, the contractor you press for a lower bid, the cheap thing you bought without asking who paid for it to be cheap. Prophetic justice that only indicts the other party is not prophetic. It is partisan with a verse attached. I have to start with my own hands.
charge: Pay what you owe, on time, to the people who counted on it. Then ask the harder question of which cries are reaching the ears of the Lord of hosts from inside your own comfort, and stop waiting for a party to answer what God has already commanded you.
